failures.title: Aston Martin AE31 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Ignition Coil Pack Degradation - 30,000-60,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The AE31's ignition coil packs are mounted directly on top of the spark plugs, deep in the V12's valley. The heat from the twin turbos bakes the coil packs over time, causing them to fail. The first symptom is usually a misfire under load, accompanied by an engine warning light. On the AE31, coil pack failure is so common that specialists recommend replacing all 12 coil packs and spark plugs as a preventative measure at 50,000 miles.
items.repairVsReplace: Coil pack replacement is a straightforward but labour-intensive job - access is limited due to the engine bay packaging. Replacing all 12 coil packs and spark plugs typically costs £1,500-£2,500 at a specialist. The coils can be replaced individually, but given the labour cost, it's false economy not to do all 12.

items.title: Cooling System Leaks - 40,000-80,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The AE31 produces significant heat - 600-770 bhp from 5.2 litres means heat management is critical. The cooling system has multiple failure points: the water pump, the coolant expansion tank, and the various plastic coolant pipes that become brittle with age and heat cycling. Coolant loss is common and must be investigated immediately - the AE31 is an all-aluminium engine and does not tolerate overheating.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump replacement is a standard repair (£800-£1,500). Coolant pipe replacement can be labour-intensive if the pipes are buried deep in the Vee. Full cooling system overhaul is recommended on high-mileage cars.

items.title: Turbocharger Oil Feed Line Leaks - 50,000-100,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The AE31's twin turbos are mounted in the Vee between the cylinder banks. The oil feed lines that supply the turbos can develop leaks over time. With turbos operating at extreme temperatures, oil leaks can lead to burnt oil smell and, in rare cases, fire risk.
items.repairVsReplace: Oil feed line replacement is labour-intensive due to the location of the turbos. Budget £1,000-£2,000 for a specialist to address this.

failures.goodYearsLine: Later AE31 engines (2019 onwards) received revised ignition coil cooling and updated coolant pipe materials. The AE31 is considered a robust unit when maintained - most issues are ancillaries rather than fundamental engine failures.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the AE31
variants.intro: The AE31 is Aston Martin's 5.2-litre twin-turbo V12, introduced in 2016 as the replacement for the naturally aspirated 6.0-litre V12 (AM28). It represents a clean-sheet design for Aston Martin, with twin-turbos, direct injection and an all-new block. Where to find your engine code: The engine code is stamped on the block - typically on a machined pad near the front of the engine on the driver's side. It also appears on your V5C logbook. Commonly confused codes: - AM28 / 6.0L V12 - the naturally aspirated 6.0L V12 used in the previous generation of DBS and DB9; very different engine, no turbos, different block architecture - M177 4.0L V8 - the Mercedes-AMG V8 used in Aston Martin's V8 lineup; much smaller, entirely different engine family - [AE31 Hybrid] - a mild-hybrid version of the AE31 used in the DBS 770 Ultimate and future V12 models; features a 48V mild-hybrid system Why fitting the wrong revision matters: The AE31 was produced in multiple power tunes - 600 bhp (DB11), 630 bhp (DB11 AMR), 715 bhp (DBS Superleggera), 745 bhp (V12 Vantage), 759 bhp (DBS 770 Ultimate). The ECU calibration, fuel injectors, turbos and intercooling all differ between tunes. Fitting the wrong spec will result in incorrect fuelling, boost control and potentially engine damage. Always match the exact power output and year.

relatives.description: AM28 6.0L V12: - the naturally aspirated 6.0-litre V12 used in the previous generation of DBS (2007-2012) and DB9. It shares the basic V12 architecture but is entirely different - no turbos, older fuel injection system, and a much lower power output (510-565 bhp). The AE31 is a clean-sheet design, not a reworked AM28.

the AE31 remains Aston Martin's flagship V12, with ongoing limited production for special editions (V12 Speedster, DBS 770 Ultimate). A hybridised version (AE31 hybrid) is expected for future models but is not yet a separate engine page.

hybrid (48V) version of the AE31 debuted in the DBS 770 Ultimate and is expected in future V12 applications. It uses the same block and turbos but adds a starter-generator and small battery pack. An engine page is pending for this variant.

M177 4.0L V8: - Aston Martin's V8 alternative, used in the V8 Vantage, DB11 V8 and DBX. It is not related mechanically to the AE31, but many buyers cross-shop the two. The M177 is considerably cheaper to replace (from £8,000) but lacks the V12's character.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement AE31 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used AE31 makes sense only with documented service history and evidence that the coil packs and cooling system have been addressed. Given the high value of the cars these engines sit in, a used engine with known history can be a viable option, but the risk of inheriting someone else's problems is real. Specialist inspection is essential. Used engines guide

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper AE31 recon addresses the ignition coil packs, cooling system components, turbo oil feed lines and all common wear items. Reconditioned units from vetted UK specialists come with a 12-24 month warranty and are the default choice for most DB11 and DBS owners. At £14,000-£18,000 supply-only, they offer the best balance of cost and peace of mind for a flagship V12 car. Reconditioned engines guide

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild is justified for high-value collectable examples (DBS 770 Ultimate, V12 Speedster) or where the original engine has matching-numbers value. A proper AE31 rebuild should include a full bottom-end rebuild, new turbochargers, upgraded cooling system, and all ancillaries. Budget £18,000-£24,000+ for a specialist rebuild. Rebuilt engines guide

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All three options can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK Aston Martin specialists, with warranties backed by the fitting workshop. Nationwide delivery and fit available. Supply & fit guide
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The AE31 sits exclusively in vehicles worth £100,000-£400,000+. A reconditioned engine at £14,000-£18,000 represents 4-15% of the vehicle's value, making replacement financially viable across the entire range. Unlike lower-value cars where replacement cost can exceed vehicle value, the AE31's host vehicles are high-value enough to justify even the most expensive rebuilt option. That said, given the significant investment, full due diligence - including specialist inspection and thorough service history review - is essential before any purchase decision.

faq.title: Aston Martin AE31 - Frequently Asked Questions

items.question: How much does an Aston Martin AE31 engine replacement cost in the UK?
items.answer: Reconditioned AE31 units start from an estimated £14,000 supply-only, with fitted prices from £15,170-£19,170+ depending on the workshop. Used engines: £9,000-£15,000 supply-only. Rebuilt units: £18,000-£24,000+ supply-only. Labour: 18-24 hours at £65-£91/hr.

items.question: What is the most common problem with the Aston Martin AE31 engine?
items.answer: Ignition coil pack degradation is the most common issue - the V12's heat bakes the coil packs, causing misfires. Specialists recommend replacing all 12 coil packs and spark plugs at 50,000 miles as preventative maintenance. Cooling system leaks (water pump, coolant pipes) and turbo oil feed line leaks are also reported. Coil pack replacement (all 12): £1,500-£2,500. Water pump replacement: £800-£1,500. Turbo oil line repair: £1,000-£2,000.

items.question: Which Aston Martin models use the AE31 engine?
items.answer: The AE31 powers Aston Martin's flagship V12 models: the DB11 V12 (2016-2023), DBS Superleggera (2018-2024), V12 Vantage (2022-2023), and limited editions like the V12 Speedster and DBS 770 Ultimate. Production continues for special models. [See full compatibility list above]

items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt AE31 engine?
items.answer: For most owners, a reconditioned AE31 with new coil packs, cooling system overhaul and turbo oil lines is the best balance of cost and reliability. Used: only with full service history and specialist inspection. Reconditioned: default for DB11 and DBS owners, 12-24 month warranty. Rebuilt: for high-value collectable examples (DBS 770 Ultimate, V12 Speedster).

items.question: How do I know if my Aston Martin has the AE31 engine?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad near the front of the engine (driver's side). The AE31 is the 5.2L twin-turbo V12 that replaced the 6.0L naturally aspirated V12. Check your V5C logbook, inspect the engine bay, or enter your registration above for instant confirmation. [Check your engine code now]

items.question: Is the AE31 based on the older 6.0L Aston Martin V12?
items.answer: No - the AE31 is a clean-sheet design. While Aston Martin's previous 6.0L V12 (AM28) was based on the Ford Duratec V6, the AE31 is an all-new engine with twin turbos, direct injection and a completely different block. They share only the V12 configuration and the Aston Martin badge. [Read about the AE31's development]
